newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania President to press on for later NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Romania President to press on for later NATO entry.

text.p: Romania's reformist leaders expressed mild disappointment on Wednesday at being left out of NATO's initial eastward expansion but vowed to get on with economic reforms to ensure the country is included next time.

The government -- and investors -- said the decision at NATO's Madrid summit to take in only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic was no tragedy and had underscored Romanian determination to close the gap with successful entrants.

But with U.S. President Bill Clinton due to sweeten the pill by making a lightning visit to Bucharest on Friday, top officials and newspapers heaped praise on French President Jacques Chirac, chief advocate of early Romanian membership.

"As far as Romania is concerned, this decision is below our expectations. Romania has done everything within its powers to prove that it is eligible for NATO membership," President Emil Constantinescu said.
"Nevertheless, Romania's extraordinary efforts, as well as its visible progress, have earned official recognition from this summit," he said in a statement issued in Madrid.
A rank outsider before the election of centrists last year, Romania was named in the NATO communique as a prime candidate, along with Slovenia, for a 1999 enlargement review.

Constantinescu said he hoped Clinton's eight-hour visit, which will include an address to Romanians at a square where students were shot dead during the 1989 anti-communist revolution, "will mark the beginning of a strategic Romanian-U.S. partnership".
Clinton's visit, the first by a U.S. leader in more than 20 years, is expected to draw large crowds.
In his speech he is certain to encourage Romanians to pursue tough reforms launched by the centrist government elected last November after seven years of leftist rule.
Constantinescu's statement also thanked "all the countries which stood at Romania's side and supported our efforts up to the very last minute here".

Chirac led a European campaign to include both Romania and Slovenia in the initial expansion and issued an impassioned plea for Washington to relent in the final hours before Tuesday's final decision was announced.
Romanian journalists in Madrid showered him with applause.
On Wednesday, he said he was sure NATO would invite both countries to join in 1999 on its 50th anniversary.
Former Prime Minister Petre Roman, now the number two state official as chairman of the upper house of parliament, praised France's efforts on Bucharest's behalf.
"France, first and foremost, through the firm voice of President Chirac, as well as Italy, Spain and Portugal, supported Romania's bid in an exemplary way," he said.
"We believe that they did so because they understand that Romania is indispensable for the future security and stability of a politically and economically united Europe."
Investors viewed Romania's exclusion from the first round as irrelevant for markets, saying they were far more concerned with the government's progress in implementing reforms.
"Foreign investors are interested in Romania's internal rather than external politics," a Western analyst said. "Moreover, the news about non-admission was not a surprise."
